deleted.title: Recover Deleted Files From an External Hard Drive
deleted.metaDescription: Deleted files from a USB external hard drive are often still there until overwritten. Stop using it and recover with free tools like PhotoRec and TestDisk.
deleted.summary: Deleting a file usually does not wipe it. It just marks its space as free, so the data stays until new files are saved over it. Check the Recycle Bin or Trash first, because many computers keep one for external drives too. If the files are not there, recovery tools are your main option.
deleted.riskNote: If the drive is healthy, recovery only reads data and changes nothing, as long as you save the results to a different drive.
stopFirst: Stop copying, saving or editing files on this drive now. New data can overwrite your deleted files.
Do not install recovery software onto the affected drive. Install it on your computer's own drive.
Do not save recovered files back to the same drive. Pick a different drive.

steps.title: Stop writing to the drive
steps.detail: Anything new saved to the drive can land on top of your deleted files. Ejecting properly also avoids creating new damage.
how: Windows: click the small USB icon in the bottom-right taskbar, then Eject. Mac: drag the drive icon to the Trash, or click the eject button in Finder.
Leave it idle until you are ready to scan.
If it is a portable SSD (a drive with no moving parts) rather than a spinning drive, read the SSD guide too, because SSDs often erase deleted data quickly.

steps.title: Check for backups and the Recycle Bin
steps.detail: The easiest recovery needs no tools at all. Many systems keep deleted files in a holding folder for a while.
how: Windows: open the Recycle Bin on the desktop and look for your files. Right-click, then Restore. Mac: click Trash in the Dock, right-click, then Put Back.
Look in File History (Windows), Time Machine (Mac), or any cloud backup such as OneDrive, iCloud or Google Drive.
Check other computers and phones where the files might have been copied.

steps.title: Prepare a destination
steps.detail: Recovered files must be saved on a different drive than the one you are rescuing, or they could overwrite what you want back.
how: Use your computer's internal drive or another drive with enough free space.
Windows: open File Explorer, This PC to see free space. Mac: select the drive in Finder and press Command-I.

steps.title: Connect the external drive directly
steps.detail: A hub or loose cable can cause drops during scanning. Keeping the drive inside its case matters because many portables encrypt data through the case's board.
how: Plug it straight into a USB port on your computer, not through a hub or a dock.
Leave it in its enclosure. You do not need to take the drive out.

steps.title: Run TestDisk for folders and names
steps.detail: TestDisk reads the drive's records, so it can often list deleted files with their original names and folders on some file systems (ways of organising files).
how: Download TestDisk from cgsecurity.org to your computer's own drive and unzip it. Windows: run testdisk_win.exe as administrator. Mac or Linux: run `sudo ./testdisk`.
Choose Create, pick your external drive by its size, accept the partition type, then choose Advanced, pick the partition and choose Undelete.
Highlight a file, press `c` to copy and choose a folder on your destination drive.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec for the rest
steps.detail: PhotoRec ignores the drive's records and scans for the recognisable shape of photos, videos and documents, so it can find files TestDisk cannot. Names are usually lost.
how: Run photorec_win.exe (Windows, as administrator) or `sudo ./photorec` (Mac or Linux).
Pick the external drive and partition, use File Opt to tick the file types you want, then choose Free if you only want deleted files.
Pick a folder on your destination drive and press `c` to start. Wait for it to say it has finished.

steps.title: Verify the results
steps.detail: Some recovered files can come back damaged, and you want to know before you wipe or reuse the drive.
how: Open a sample of each file type to check it works fully.
Keep the external drive untouched until you are happy with the results.

deleted.callPro: If the drive starts clicking or disconnecting, or the files are irreplaceable and scans find nothing, stop and ask a professional.

faq.q: Are deleted files on an external drive in the Recycle Bin?
faq.a: Often yes. Windows and macOS usually keep a Recycle Bin or Trash for external hard drives, so check there first. If they are not there, stop writing to the drive and use recovery software.

faq.q: Do I need to take the drive out of its case?
faq.a: No, scan it while it is still in its case. Many portables have USB built onto the drive or encrypt data through the case's board, so removing it can make the data unreadable.

faq.q: Why are recovered file names missing?
faq.a: PhotoRec finds files by what they contain, not by the drive's records, so names and folders are often lost. TestDisk can sometimes keep them.

formatted.title: Recover Files From a Formatted External Drive
formatted.metaDescription: Formatted your external hard drive? Quick format is often recoverable, full format on Windows is not. Learn which tools to use and what to avoid.
formatted.summary: A quick format erases the drive's table of contents but usually leaves your data in place, so recovery is often possible. A full format on Windows Vista or newer writes zeros over everything, and that data is gone for good.
formatted.riskNote: Scanning only reads the drive, but saving anything new onto it can overwrite what is left.
stopFirst: Do not copy any new files onto the formatted drive. New data overwrites what you want back.
Do not format it again, even to a different file system (a different way of organising files).
Do not install recovery software onto the formatted drive.

steps.title: Figure out the format type
steps.detail: A quick format only erases the index, so files can come back. A full format on Windows Vista or newer overwrites everything with zeros, and those files cannot be recovered.
how: Think back: did the format finish in seconds or a few minutes? That was quick. Did it take hours? That was full.
Windows: the Format window had a Quick Format tick box. Mac: Erase is normally quick unless you chose Security Options and moved the slider towards Most Secure.
If you are not sure, carry on. Scanning is safe.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: Any new copy or backup can land on the space your old files used.
how: Windows: click the USB icon in the taskbar, then Eject. Mac: click the eject button next to the drive in Finder.
Do not set it up again for a new backup or file copy, even if a program asks.

steps.title: Connect it directly
steps.detail: A direct connection avoids drops during a long scan. Keeping the drive in its case matters because many portables encrypt data through the case's board.
how: Plug it into a USB port on your computer, not through a hub, and leave it in its enclosure.
Prepare a separate drive with enough free space for the results.

steps.title: Run TestDisk
steps.detail: TestDisk searches for the lost partition (the section of the drive that holds your files) and may restore your folders with their original names, especially after a quick format.
how: Download TestDisk from cgsecurity.org to your computer's own drive and unzip it. Windows: run testdisk_win.exe as administrator. Mac or Linux: `sudo ./testdisk`.
Choose Create, pick your external drive by its size, accept the partition type, then choose Analyse and Quick Search.
If your old partition appears, press `p` to list its files, copy what you need with `c` to your other drive, or choose Write to restore it.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec if TestDisk cannot help
steps.detail: PhotoRec scans for the shape of known file types and saves them to your other drive. Expect generic names that you sort afterwards.
how: Run photorec_win.exe (Windows, as administrator) or `sudo ./photorec` (Mac or Linux).
Pick the external drive, choose Whole disk, then pick a folder on your other drive and press `c`.
Expect hours for a large drive.

steps.title: Check your files
steps.detail: This tells you whether the drive was fully formatted or overwritten, or is an SSD that erased the freed space on its own.
how: Open a few of each type. Photos should show completely and documents should open without errors.
If many files are blank or damaged, stop. Read the SSD guide if your drive has no moving parts.

formatted.callPro: If the drive drops out or makes noises, or the data is critical and scans come up empty, stop and ask a professional.

faq.q: Can I recover data after a full format?
faq.a: On Windows Vista and later, no. A full format writes zeros over the drive. A quick format is often recoverable.

faq.q: Did reformatting for a Mac or PC erase my files?
faq.a: Reformatting to another file system counts as a format. If it was a quick format, the old data is just hidden. Stop using the drive and scan it right away.

faq.q: Will I keep my folders?
faq.a: Sometimes with TestDisk. With PhotoRec, files usually come back sorted by type with generic names.

not-detected.title: External Hard Drive Not Showing Up or Detected
not-detected.metaDescription: External hard drive not showing up or recognized? Check cable, port and power first, then learn about enclosure faults, soldered USB ports and encryption.
not-detected.summary: An external drive is a hard drive inside a case, plus a small bridge board that turns USB into the drive's own connection. The fault could be the cable, the port, the bridge board or the drive itself. Start with cheap, safe checks.
not-detected.riskNote: Cable and software checks are safe, but taking the drive out of its case can lock encrypted data or damage it.
stopFirst: If your computer offers to Initialize or Format the drive, click Cancel. Either can erase your data.
Do not keep plugging and unplugging it if you hear clicking or the drive feels hot. That adds wear.
Do not open the drive's case yet. Many portable drives are encrypted or have USB soldered to the drive, so removing it can make data unreadable.

steps.title: Try another cable and port
steps.detail: USB cables and ports fail often, and swapping them costs nothing.
how: Use a different USB cable, ideally the one that came with the drive, and plug it directly into the computer, not into a hub.
Try a different USB port, and for desktop-style drives check the power adapter is firmly plugged in at both ends.

steps.title: Try a second computer
steps.detail: This tells you whether the problem is your computer or the drive.
how: Plug the drive into another computer, ideally one with a different operating system.
Works elsewhere: the problem is your computer, its drivers or its port. Fails everywhere: the drive or its bridge board is the likely cause.

steps.title: Check Disk Management or Disk Utility
steps.detail: These tools show drives that the computer can see but cannot use yet, for example a drive with no letter.
how: Windows: right-click the Start button, choose Disk Management. Mac: open Finder, Applications, Utilities, Disk Utility, then View, Show All Devices.
Find your drive by its size. If it says Raw, Unallocated or Not Initialized, do not click Initialize, Format or Erase.
Use TestDisk instead, ideally on an image (an exact copy of the whole drive saved as a file).

steps.title: Listen and feel
steps.detail: What the drive sounds like tells you whether the fault is a simple one.
how: With the drive connected, rest a fingertip on it. A soft hum or vibration means it spins.
Clicking, grinding or complete silence points to a drive fault. Unplug it and read our clicking or no-power guide.

steps.title: Understand the enclosure
steps.detail: If the computer sees a USB device but no storage, the bridge board may have failed while the drive inside is fine.
how: Windows: in Device Manager, look under Disk drives and Universal Serial Bus controllers. Mac: Apple menu, About This Mac, System Report, USB.
Listed as a USB device but with no disk: suspect the bridge board. Do not assume the drive inside is bad.

steps.title: Know the risk of opening the case
steps.detail: Many WD portables, and some other brands, have the USB port built right onto the drive's board, and many WD My Passport and My Book drives encrypt data through the case's bridge board (the small board that turns USB into the drive's own connection). Taking the drive out can leave you with unreadable data.
how: Do not open the case or remove the drive unless you know the exact model has a normal SATA connector and no hardware encryption.
Search the model number plus 'encryption' or 'SATA' to check, or ask a recovery professional.

steps.title: If it is readable, check health and image it
steps.detail: An image (an exact copy of the whole drive saved as a file) lets you recover from a copy and leave a weak drive alone. SMART is the drive's own health record.
how: Read SMART with CrystalDiskInfo (Windows) or `smartctl -a /dev/sdX` (Mac or Linux). Some USB cases hide SMART, so a missing report does not mean it is fine.
If errors show, follow our imaging guide with ddrescue. Always type the failing drive first and the empty destination second. If you swap them, the copy erases your data.
Then run TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image file.

not-detected.callPro: If it is not detected on any computer with a good cable, or it is a soldered or encrypted portable with important data, stop and ask a professional.

faq.q: Can I just take the drive out and plug it into my computer?
faq.a: Sometimes, but not always. Some portables have no standard SATA port, and some encrypt data using the original case's board, so the data may look blank outside it.

faq.q: How do I tell a bad enclosure from a bad drive?
faq.a: If the drive spins and sounds normal but no disk appears on any computer, the bridge board may be bad. Clicking, grinding or silence points to the drive itself.

faq.q: Should I format it when Windows asks?
faq.a: No. Formatting can erase the data you want to save. Click Cancel and use TestDisk first.

clicking.title: External Hard Drive Clicking, Grinding or Beeping
clicking.metaDescription: External hard drive clicking, grinding or beeping? It is likely mechanical failure. Learn what not to do, why not to open it, and when to get help.
clicking.summary: Clicking, grinding or beeping from the drive inside usually means the read/write heads (the tiny arms that read the disk) or the motor are failing. Each time you power it on, the damage can grow, and portable drives are easily hurt by drops.
clicking.riskNote: Mechanical faults worsen with every power-up, and real repairs need a cleanroom.
stopFirst: Unplug it and leave it off. Do not keep trying, because each power-up can scratch the disk inside.
Do not use the freezer trick, tap it or shake it. These are myths that can do harm.
Never open the drive itself. Dust ruins the disk, and it needs a cleanroom.
Do not run recovery scans, CHKDSK or any repair tool on it. Heavy reading stresses a failing drive, and making a copy (see below) is the only DIY step worth trying.

steps.title: Unplug it now
steps.detail: Switching off stops damage growing. What you heard also helps an expert.
how: Unplug the USB cable, and the power adapter if there is one.
Write down what you heard: clicking, grinding, beeping or nothing, and when it started.

steps.title: Judge how much the data matters
steps.detail: Home attempts can lower a lab's odds. Knowing the value of your files tells you whether the risk is worth it.
how: Irreplaceable files such as family photos: skip to the last step and contact a professional.
Replaceable files or you accept the risk: read on, and plan for one careful try at most.

steps.title: Be careful about the enclosure
steps.detail: Taking the drive out of its case can destroy access to the data even if the drive is fine. Many WD portables, and some other brands, have the USB port built right onto the drive's board, and many WD My Passport and My Book drives encrypt data through the case's bridge board (the small board that turns USB into the drive's own connection).
how: Do not remove the drive from its case.
Do not move it to another case either.

steps.title: Try one careful connection with good power
steps.detail: Weak USB power can cause clicking on some portables, so one try with better power is reasonable. Do not retry if it fails.
how: Use one good, short USB cable. If the drive has its own power adapter or a Y-cable (a cable with two USB plugs), use it.
Plug into a USB port directly on the computer.
If it spins and appears, go straight to making an image. If it clicks again, unplug.

steps.title: Get the copy direction right
steps.detail: Imaging means copying everything on the drive to a file. In ddrescue or HDDSuperClone (free tools for Linux), the clicking drive is the source and a healthy drive is the destination. Getting this wrong is very costly.
how: Boot a Linux live USB (a USB stick that runs its own system without installing anything) on a computer, plug in the clicking drive and a healthy destination drive.
In a terminal run `lsblk` to see both drives by size. Note the name of each, such as sdb and sdc.

Run `sudo ddrescue -n /dev/sdX /mnt/backup/disk.img /mnt/backup/disk.map`, where sdX is the clicking drive. Always type the failing drive first and the empty destination second. If you swap them, the copy erases your data.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: The image can be searched again and again, so the clicking drive does not need to run any more.
how: Power off and unplug the clicking drive.
Run TestDisk on the image to list folders, then PhotoRec if names are lost.
Save recovered files to a third drive.

steps.title: Stop at the first relapse and call a pro
steps.detail: If the clicking returns or the drive vanishes, more tries cut down what a lab can save. A cleanroom lab can swap the damaged parts.
how: Power off at the first stall or click.
Pack the drive in a padded box and ask a few labs for a price and their policy if they cannot recover anything.

clicking.callPro: If it clicks, grinds, beeps or will not spin and the data matters, stop and ask a professional with a cleanroom.

faq.q: Is clicking caused by the USB case?
faq.a: Usually no. The sound comes from the drive's moving parts. A weak power supply can trigger it on some portables, so trying a better power source once is reasonable.

faq.q: Can I put it in the freezer?
faq.a: No. It is a myth that can cause water damage from condensation. Experts advise against it.

faq.q: Can I swap it into another case?
faq.a: It will not fix a mechanical fault, and some drives have soldered USB or encryption tied to the original board. Avoid it unless you know the exact model.

no-power.title: External Hard Drive Not Spinning or Won't Power On
no-power.metaDescription: External hard drive dead, no lights, not spinning, or smells burnt? Check the cable and power, learn about bridge board faults, and know when to stop.
no-power.summary: If an external drive has no lights or sound, the cause may be a bad cable, a dead power adapter, a failed bridge board (the small board that turns USB into the drive's own connection) or a failed drive. A burnt smell points to an electrical fault, so stop trying.
no-power.riskNote: Cable and adapter checks are safe, but repeated attempts on a drive with an electrical or motor fault can make things worse.
stopFirst: Unplug it if you smell burning or see scorch marks. Do not power it up again.
Do not keep switching it on and off hoping it starts.
Do not use the freezer trick, and never open the drive. It needs a cleanroom.
Do not use a power adapter that is not the one it came with. The wrong voltage can burn the board.

steps.title: Look and smell for damage
steps.detail: Damage you can see can save you from making things worse.
how: Unplug everything. Look at the USB port on the drive for bent, loose or broken pins.
Sniff for a burnt smell. Loose or broken ports are common on portables.

steps.title: Check the power source
steps.detail: Many dead-looking drives only have a bad cable, adapter or outlet.
how: Try one other USB cable and port, then one other computer.
For desktop-style drives, check the wall adapter is the original one and test the outlet with a lamp.

steps.title: Look for lights and listen
steps.detail: The light and sound show how far the drive gets.
how: Plug it in and watch for an LED light on the drive. Rest a fingertip on it for 10 seconds.
Lights but no hum: suspect the drive or motor. No lights: suspect cable, power or bridge board.
Switch off after one try.

steps.title: Understand what might be inside
steps.detail: A bridge board fault can leave a healthy drive inside, but swapping parts can make data unreadable. Many WD portables, and some other brands, have the USB port built right onto the drive's board, and many WD My Passport and My Book drives encrypt data through the case's bridge board (the small board that turns USB into the drive's own connection).
how: Do not try swapping the bridge board or putting the drive in another case.
Search your exact model number plus 'encryption' to see if it uses hardware encryption.

steps.title: Avoid DIY surgery on soldered or encrypted models
steps.detail: Prying the case can break clips and snap the thin connector, and gives no benefit if the data is encrypted.
how: Do not pry the drive out unless you know it has a normal SATA connector and is not hardware encrypted.
If unsure, leave the case closed and ask a recovery professional.

steps.title: If it spins and appears, image it
steps.detail: An image (an exact copy of the whole drive saved as a file) lets you recover files without running a shaky drive again and again.
how: Follow our imaging guide with ddrescue onto a different drive. Always type the failing drive first and the empty destination second. If you swap them, the copy erases your data.
Then run TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image file.

steps.title: Stop if it stays dead
steps.detail: If nothing works after a good cable and power source, it needs hardware repair by a professional. More tries can only harm it.
how: Unplug it and pack it in a padded box.
Tell the lab what you saw, heard and smelled.

no-power.callPro: If there are no lights or spin after good cable and power checks, or there is a burnt smell, stop and ask a professional.

faq.q: No lights at all. Is the drive dead?
faq.a: Not necessarily. A broken cable, adapter, USB port or bridge board can look the same. Try other cables and computers before giving up.

faq.q: Can I take the drive out and connect it directly?
faq.a: Only if it has a standard SATA connector and is not encrypted by the case. Many portables do not, so check the exact model first.

faq.q: Is a loose USB port fixable?
faq.a: It can be, but soldering takes skill, and a poor repair can damage the board. Ask an expert for valuable data.

liquid-fire.title: Water, Liquid or Fire Damaged External Drive
liquid-fire.metaDescription: External hard drive got wet, flooded or burned? Do not power it on, do not use rice or heat. Here is what to do and why a professional is the safe choice.
liquid-fire.summary: Liquid can short the bridge board and the drive's own board, and corrosion starts quickly. Fire and heat can warp parts. Powering it on can destroy what is left, so keep it off and get professional help.
liquid-fire.riskNote: Power, heat or opening the case can turn damage that could be fixed into permanent loss.
stopFirst: Do not plug it in or power it on, not even once to test.
Do not dry it with a hair dryer, oven or heater, and do not put it in rice. Heat can warp parts, and rice adds dust without drying the inside.
Do not open the drive or try to clean the disk.
Do not shake it or rinse it to remove dirt or salt.

steps.title: Unplug and leave it off
steps.detail: Power into a wet drive can short the board and scratch the disk.
how: Pull out the USB cable and any power adapter.
Do not plug a wet adapter into the wall. That is a shock risk.
Do not press any buttons to test it.

steps.title: Note what happened
steps.detail: What touched the drive decides how quickly it corrodes.
how: Write down whether it was clean water, salt water, a sugary drink, flood mud, smoke or flames, and when.
Take a photo of the drive as it is now, if safe.

steps.title: Do not take the drive out of the case yourself
steps.detail: Prying can break parts. Many WD portables, and some other brands, have the USB port built right onto the drive's board, and many WD My Passport and My Book drives encrypt data through the case's bridge board (the small board that turns USB into the drive's own connection). Separating them can make the data unreadable.
how: Leave the drive in its case, exactly as it is.
Do not wipe or rinse it.

steps.title: Pack it carefully
steps.detail: Knocks can scratch a stopped disk, and heat can warp parts.
how: Wrap it in a soft cloth and put it in a padded box.
If it came from a flood and is muddy or salty, put it in a sealed plastic bag and keep it damp instead of letting it dry.

steps.title: Contact a professional soon
steps.detail: Corrosion spreads with time, so waiting lowers the odds. Only a lab with a cleanroom can safely clean and read it.
how: Search for data recovery labs that use a cleanroom and ask for a quote before shipping.
Ask about their price and their policy if they cannot recover anything.
Send it with tracking and insurance.

liquid-fire.callPro: Liquid, smoke or fire damage should go to a professional with a cleanroom before anyone powers the drive on.

faq.q: Can rice dry out a wet external drive?
faq.a: No. Rice does not remove moisture well and can add dust. Keep the drive off and get professional help.

faq.q: It only got a splash. Can I try it once it dries?
faq.a: It is a gamble. Residue can short the board and a power-up can scratch the disk, so use a professional for important data.

faq.q: Will the case protect the drive?
faq.a: Not against liquid. Most cases are not sealed, and water can reach the board and the drive.

corrupted.title: Fix a Corrupted or Unreadable External Hard Drive
corrupted.metaDescription: External hard drive shows RAW, asks to format, or has read errors? Image it with ddrescue first, then recover files with TestDisk or PhotoRec on the copy.
corrupted.summary: Corruption often follows pulling the cable without ejecting, a power cut or failing parts. It means the drive's records of where files are got damaged, and the files are often still there. Do not run repair tools on the original first, because they can change your data.
corrupted.riskNote: The drive may be weak, and repair tools such as CHKDSK on the original can change data before you have a copy.
stopFirst: Do not run CHKDSK, fsck or Disk Utility's First Aid on the original before copying your data.
Do not click Format when the computer says the drive needs formatting.
Do not install recovery software onto the affected drive or save files back to it.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: Extra reads and writes can worsen damage.
how: Windows: click the USB icon in the taskbar, then Eject. Mac: click the eject button next to the drive in Finder.
If it clicks or grinds, unplug it and read our clicking guide instead.

steps.title: Check its health
steps.detail: SMART is the drive's own health record. It shows whether the disk is wearing out.
how: Windows: install and open CrystalDiskInfo and read the Health Status. Mac or Linux: in a terminal run `smartctl -a /dev/sdX`.
Some USB cases hide SMART, so a missing report does not mean the drive is fine.

steps.title: Try a different cable and port
steps.detail: A bad cable can look just like corruption, and it costs nothing to rule out.
how: Plug directly into the computer, not through a hub, with a different cable.
Keep the drive in its case, because many WD drives encrypt data through the case's board.

steps.title: Get a destination drive
steps.detail: An image (an exact copy of the whole drive saved as a file) needs as much room as the original.
how: Check the damaged drive's size in File Explorer or Disk Utility.
Use a different drive with at least that much free space.

steps.title: Image with ddrescue
steps.detail: ddrescue copies the drive while skipping unreadable spots and returning to them later, which saves the most data and stresses the drive the least.
how: Boot a Linux live USB if needed, open a terminal and run `lsblk` to identify both drives.

Run `sudo ddrescue -n /dev/sdX /mnt/backup/disk.img /mnt/backup/disk.map`, where sdX is the damaged drive. Always type the failing drive first and the empty destination second. If you swap them, the copy erases your data.
Keep the map file so you can stop and resume. HDDSuperClone is an alternative on Linux.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: The image is expendable, so you can try again if something goes wrong.
how: Run `sudo testdisk disk.img` to rebuild partitions or list files, and copy them to another drive.
If folders are too damaged, run `sudo photorec disk.img`. Never work on the original.

corrupted.callPro: If imaging keeps stalling, the drive makes noises, or the data is critical, stop and ask a professional.

faq.q: Should I run CHKDSK first?
faq.a: No. It can rewrite damaged data. Image the drive first and repair or recover from the copy.

faq.q: Why does it say the drive is RAW?
faq.a: The computer cannot read the drive's file system, which is its way of organising files, often because of an unsafe unplug or damage. TestDisk can often restore it.

faq.q: Why can't I see SMART data?
faq.a: Many USB cases do not pass it through. That is common and does not mean the drive is healthy.

encrypted.title: Recover Data From an Encrypted External Drive
encrypted.metaDescription: Locked out of an encrypted external drive such as WD My Passport, BitLocker or Mac encryption? Find your key first. Without it, recovery is unrealistic.
encrypted.summary: Many external drives encrypt (scramble) their data, either with software such as BitLocker or Mac's built-in encryption, or with hardware encryption, as on many WD My Passport and My Book drives. Without the password or recovery key, recovery is not realistic.
encrypted.riskNote: Unlocking with a known key is low risk, but taking a hardware-encrypted drive out of its case can make the data unreadable.
stopFirst: Do not remove the drive from its case if it uses hardware encryption. The key may be tied to the bridge board, and a different adapter can show unreadable data.
Do not format or reset it. That destroys the key and the data.
Do not trust tools or people claiming to crack or brute-force strong encryption.

steps.title: Find out what kind of encryption it is
steps.detail: Each kind unlocks differently, so you need to know which you have first.
how: Look at the model name on the drive. WD My Passport and My Book often use hardware encryption, even if you never set a password.
Windows: a padlock on the drive icon means BitLocker To Go. Mac: a password prompt when you plug it in means Mac encryption. VeraCrypt asks for a password in its own app.

steps.title: Find your recovery key
steps.detail: The recovery key is a long backup code made when encryption was turned on, which unlocks the drive if the password fails.
how: BitLocker: sign in at account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey, or check a work or school account, a printed page or a saved file.
Mac: use the password you set, which may be saved in Keychain Access (Applications, Utilities).

steps.title: Use the vendor's unlock tool
steps.detail: Hardware-encrypted drives are unlocked by the maker's own software, using the same case that encrypted them.
how: For password-protected WD drives, download WD Security or WD Drive Utilities from the WD support site.
Keep the drive in its original case, plug it in, open the software and type your password.

steps.title: Keep the original case and cable
steps.detail: With hardware encryption the key lives in the bridge board, so a different adapter or a direct SATA connection can show scrambled data.
how: Do not move the drive to another case or connect it directly to a computer.
Keep the original USB cable and, if there is one, the power adapter.

steps.title: Copy data after unlocking
steps.detail: Once unlocked, files can be copied out normally. If the drive is also faulty, an image (an exact copy of the whole drive saved as a file) protects you.
how: Copy your files to a different drive and open a few to check them.

If the drive is also faulty, follow our imaging guide with ddrescue while it is unlocked and still in its case. Always type the failing drive first and the empty destination second. If you swap them, the copy erases your data.

steps.title: Accept the limit if the key is lost
steps.detail: Without the password or recovery key, strong encryption cannot be broken in practice, and recovery tools will only find scrambled data.
how: If you have no password and no key, the data cannot realistically be recovered.
If the drive is damaged and you do hold the key, ask a professional.

encrypted.callPro: If the drive or its board is damaged and you hold the password or key, a professional may be able to help. Without the key, no one can realistically recover the data.

faq.q: Why is my WD drive unreadable outside its case?
faq.a: Many WD My Passport and My Book drives encrypt data using a key tied to the bridge board (the small board that turns USB into the drive's own connection). A different adapter can leave the data unreadable.

faq.q: Where is my BitLocker recovery key?
faq.a: Often in your Microsoft account online, a work or school account, a printed page or a saved file.

faq.q: Can someone crack it for me?
faq.a: Not realistically. Strong encryption is designed to resist this, so be wary of anyone who says otherwise.

deleted.title: Recover Deleted Files From an Internal Hard Drive
deleted.metaDescription: Deleted files on a hard drive are often still there until overwritten. Learn how to stop the damage and safely recover them with free tools like PhotoRec.
deleted.summary: When you delete a file, the computer usually does not wipe it. It just marks the space as free to reuse. Your file stays on the disk until something new is saved over it, so the sooner you stop using the drive, the better your chances.
deleted.riskNote: If the drive is healthy, recovery only reads data and changes nothing, as long as you save the results to a different drive.
stopFirst: Stop saving, downloading, installing or browsing on this drive right now. Anything new can overwrite your deleted files.
Do not install recovery software onto this drive. Install it on a different drive, or run it from a USB stick.
Do not save recovered files back onto this drive. Always choose a different drive as the destination.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: Every minute the computer runs, it quietly saves small files, and those can land on the space your deleted files used. Stopping now protects them.
how: If the drive is your main Windows or Mac drive: save nothing, close your programs, then shut the computer down. Windows: Start menu, Power, Shut down. Mac: Apple menu, Shut Down.
If it is a second internal drive, just stop saving or downloading to it until the recovery is done.

steps.title: Check the Recycle Bin or Trash first
steps.detail: Deleted files often go to a holding folder first, and restoring from there is instant and risk free. Backups can also hold a copy.
how: Windows: double-click Recycle Bin on the desktop, right-click your file, choose Restore. Mac: click Trash in the Dock, right-click the file, choose Put Back.
Windows: also try right-click the folder, Properties, Previous Versions (this uses File History). Mac: open Time Machine from the menu bar and browse back in time.
Check any cloud backup you use, such as OneDrive, iCloud or Google Drive, for a Deleted or Recently deleted section.

steps.title: Prepare a second drive
steps.detail: Recovered files must be saved somewhere other than the drive you are rescuing, or they could overwrite the very data you want back.
how: Get an external drive or USB stick with at least as much free space as the files you want back.
Plug it in and check it opens normally. Windows: File Explorer, This PC. Mac: Finder sidebar.

steps.title: Run recovery from a USB stick or another computer
steps.detail: Recovery tools only read your drive, but installing them on it could overwrite your files. Running them from a USB stick or a second computer keeps the original drive untouched.
how: Simplest: shut down, remove the drive, and attach it to a second computer as an extra drive (a USB adapter or dock works).
Or boot from a live USB (a USB stick that starts its own small copy of Linux so nothing is installed). Our guide shows how to make one.
On the Linux desktop, open a terminal (a window where you type commands) from the menu.

steps.title: Try TestDisk first to get names and folders back
steps.detail: TestDisk reads the drive's records of what was stored where, so it can often list deleted files with their original names and folders.
how: In the terminal, type `sudo testdisk` and press Enter.
Choose Create (new log), pick your drive with the arrow keys, press Enter, pick the partition type it suggests (usually Intel or EFI GPT), then choose Advanced.
Select the partition holding your files, choose Undelete, highlight the file, press `c` to copy, and pick the folder on your second drive.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec if names are lost
steps.detail: PhotoRec ignores the records and scans the raw drive for the recognisable shape of photos, documents and other file types. You get the contents back, but usually with generic names.
how: In the terminal, type `sudo photorec` and press Enter.
Pick the drive, then the partition, then choose File Opt to tick only the file types you want, which speeds things up.
Choose the folder on your second drive as the destination and press `c` to start. Wait until it says it has finished.

steps.title: Check your recovered files
steps.detail: Some recovered files can be damaged, and you want to know that before you wipe or reuse the drive.
how: Open a handful of files of each type, such as a photo, a document and a video, and make sure they open fully.
Keep the original drive untouched until you are happy with the results.
If you are unsure whether the drive itself is healthy, see our health check guide.

deleted.callPro: If the drive starts making odd noises or disappears, or the files are very valuable and recovery fails, stop and call a professional.

faq.q: Can I get back files I emptied from the Recycle Bin?
faq.a: Often yes. Emptying the bin only marks the space as free, so stop using the drive right away. Some newer drives (called SMR drives) tidy up freed space on their own, which lowers the odds.

faq.q: Why did my recovered files lose their names?
faq.a: PhotoRec finds files by what they contain, not by the drive's records, so names and folders are not saved. TestDisk can sometimes keep names if those records are still intact.

faq.q: Does it matter that I kept using the computer after deleting?
faq.a: It lowers the odds a little, because new data may have landed on the freed space. Stop now and recover what is left.

formatted.title: Recover Files From a Formatted Hard Drive
formatted.metaDescription: Accidentally formatted a hard drive? Quick format is often recoverable, full format on Windows is not. Learn what to do and which free tools to use.
formatted.summary: A quick format wipes the drive's table of contents but leaves most of your data in place, so recovery is often possible. A full format on Windows Vista or newer writes zeros over everything, and that data is gone for good.
formatted.riskNote: Recovery software only reads the drive, but saving anything new onto it can destroy what is left.
stopFirst: Do not copy, save or install anything onto the formatted drive. New data overwrites what you want back.
Do not format it again, and do not reinstall Windows or macOS onto it.
Do not install recovery software onto the formatted drive. Use a different drive.

steps.title: Work out which kind of format you did
steps.detail: A quick format only erases the index, so files can come back. A full format on Windows Vista or newer overwrites everything with zeros, so nothing can come back. Knowing which one you did sets your expectations.
how: Think back: did the format finish in seconds or a few minutes? That was a quick format. Did it run for hours? That was a full format.
On Windows, the Format window had a Quick Format tick box. If it was ticked, it was quick. On a Mac, Erase is normally quick unless you chose Security Options and moved the slider toward Most Secure.
If you are not sure, carry on. Scanning is safe, and the results will tell you.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: If you reinstalled the operating system onto it, the install has already overwritten some of the old data. Any more writing makes it worse.
how: Do not copy files onto it, install programs, or start a new backup.
If it is your main drive and the computer is running, shut it down: Windows Start, Power, Shut down; Mac Apple menu, Shut Down.

steps.title: Attach it to a second computer
steps.detail: This lets you scan the drive without the drive running anything. You also need a separate drive to save results on.
how: Shut down, unplug the drive and connect it to a second computer as an extra drive, using a USB adapter or dock if needed.
Or boot from a live USB (a USB stick that runs its own small copy of Linux without installing anything).
Get a different drive with enough free space for everything you want back.

steps.title: Try TestDisk to restore the old structure
steps.detail: TestDisk searches for the lost partition (a section of the drive that holds your files) and may bring back folders with their original names. It works best after a quick format.
how: In a terminal, type `sudo testdisk` and press Enter. On Windows, run testdisk_win.exe as administrator.
Choose Create, pick the drive, accept the partition type it suggests, then choose Analyse and Quick Search.
If it finds your old partition, press `p` to list its files and check they look right. Then choose Write to restore it, or copy the files out with `c` first if you prefer.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec if TestDisk finds nothing
steps.detail: PhotoRec scans the whole drive for the recognisable shape of photos, documents and other known file types. Names and folders are usually lost, but the contents come back.
how: Type `sudo photorec` (Windows: run photorec_win.exe as administrator) and pick the drive.
Choose Whole disk, then the file system type Other (for FAT, NTFS, exFAT) or ext2/3/4 as needed.
Pick a folder on your second drive and press `c`. This can take hours for a big drive.

steps.title: Check what you got
steps.detail: This tells you whether the drive was fully formatted, overwritten, or maybe one of the newer SMR drives that clear freed space on their own.
how: Open a few files of each type. Photos should show the whole picture, and documents should open without errors.
If many files are blank or damaged, the data was probably overwritten. Stop there rather than running more tools.
Sort the recovered files into folders and make a backup of the good ones right away.

formatted.callPro: If the drive makes noises, is not detected, or the data is critical and software scans fail, stop and ask a professional.

faq.q: Can I recover data after a full format?
faq.a: On Windows Vista and newer, no. A full format writes zeros over the whole disk. A quick format is a different story and is often recoverable.

faq.q: Did reinstalling Windows destroy my files?
faq.a: It overwrote part of the drive, so some files are lost. Others may still be there, so stop using it and scan it from another computer with PhotoRec.

faq.q: Will I get my folders and file names back?
faq.a: Sometimes with TestDisk. With PhotoRec, files usually come back with generic names and are sorted by type.

not-detected.title: Hard Drive Not Showing Up or Not Detected
not-detected.metaDescription: Hard drive not detected or not showing in Windows or Mac? Check cables, ports and Disk Management first, then recover data without more damage.
not-detected.summary: A drive that does not show up may have a loose cable, a bad port, a lost partition (the section that holds your files), or a real hardware fault. The first checks are simple and safe. If the drive is silent, clicking or very hot, the cause may be physical.
not-detected.riskNote: Cable and software checks are safe, but powering a failing drive on and off again and again can make the damage worse.
stopFirst: Do not keep switching the drive on and off to see if it comes back. Each try adds wear if it is failing.
If your computer offers to Initialize or Format the drive, click Cancel. Either one can erase your data.
Do not open the drive. The inside needs a cleanroom, and ordinary dust ruins it.

steps.title: Listen and feel
steps.detail: What the drive sounds like tells you whether this is a simple problem or a physical one. A healthy drive spins up with a soft hum.
how: With the drive connected and the computer on, listen closely and rest a fingertip lightly on the drive.
Soft hum or gentle vibration: it is spinning, so carry on to the next step.
Clicking, grinding or beeping: unplug it and read our clicking guide. Burning smell or silence: unplug it and read our no-power guide.

steps.title: Check the BIOS or UEFI
steps.detail: The BIOS (also called UEFI) is a screen built into your computer that lists every drive it can physically see, before Windows or macOS starts. If the drive is listed there, the hardware is working.
how: Restart the computer and tap the BIOS key as it starts. Common keys are Del, F2, F10 or F12; the startup screen often shows which one.
Look in the Storage, Boot or SATA information section for your drive's model name and size.
Listed correctly: the problem is probably software or the partition. Not listed: go to the next step. Leave the BIOS with Esc without changing anything.

steps.title: Swap the cable and port
steps.detail: Bad cables and ports cause many drive-not-found problems, and changing them is free and safe.
how: Shut down and unplug the power. Open the case if it is a desktop.
Swap the thin SATA data cable for another one and plug into a different SATA port on the motherboard. Press each connector in firmly.
Check the wider power connector is firmly seated, or try a different one from the power supply. Then start the computer and look in the BIOS again.

steps.title: Look in Disk Management or Disk Utility
steps.detail: These built-in tools show drives that the system can see but cannot use yet, such as a drive with no letter or no recognised file system.
how: Windows: right-click the Start button, choose Disk Management. Mac: open Finder, Applications, Utilities, Disk Utility, then View, Show All Devices.
Find your drive by its size. If it says Raw, Unallocated or Not Initialized, that is fine. Do not click Initialize, Format or Erase.
If it is listed, note what it says and move on to the health check.

steps.title: Check drive health
steps.detail: The drive keeps its own health record, called SMART. Reading it shows whether the drive is failing, before you stress it any further.
how: Windows: install CrystalDiskInfo and open it. Look at the big Health Status box: Good is fine, Caution or Bad means it is failing.
Mac or Linux: in a terminal, run `smartctl -a /dev/sdX` (replace sdX with your drive, which `lsblk` shows).
Look for Reallocated, Pending or Uncorrectable sector counts above zero. Those mean the surface is wearing out.

steps.title: Copy the data off, or make an image first
steps.detail: If the drive works but shows signs of weakness, an image (an exact copy of the whole drive saved as a file) lets you try recovery on the copy and leave the weak original alone.
how: Get a different drive at least as big as the failing one.
Follow our imaging guide to copy the drive with ddrescue. Always type the failing drive first and the empty destination second. If you swap them, the copy erases your data.
Then run TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image file, not on the original drive.

steps.title: Stop if it still does not appear
steps.detail: A drive that cannot be seen in the BIOS after a cable swap has most likely failed in its circuit board or inside. Further tries risk more damage.
how: Unplug the drive and put it somewhere safe.
Do not try a replacement circuit board yourself. Each board holds a small ROM chip with data unique to that drive, and it must be moved onto the new board by a specialist.
Contact a professional recovery lab and describe what you tried.

not-detected.callPro: If the drive is missing from the BIOS after a new cable and port, or it makes any unusual noise, stop and ask a professional with a cleanroom.

faq.q: My drive shows up but says Raw or needs formatting. What now?
faq.a: Do not format it. The drive's file records are probably damaged, and TestDisk or PhotoRec can often still reach your files, ideally working on an image (a full copy of the drive).

faq.q: Could it just be a cable?
faq.a: Yes, that is very common. Try another cable, another port and another power connector before assuming the drive is dead.

faq.q: Can I fix it by swapping the circuit board?
faq.a: Not as a DIY fix. Each board has a ROM chip with data unique to that drive, which must be moved onto the new board, so leave it to specialists.

clicking.title: Hard Drive Clicking, Grinding or Beeping
clicking.metaDescription: A clicking, grinding or beeping hard drive is failing mechanically. Learn what not to do, why the freezer trick is a myth, and when DIY is reasonable.
clicking.summary: Clicking, grinding or beeping usually means the moving parts inside, such as the read/write heads (the tiny arms that read the disk), are damaged or stuck. Every extra power-up can scratch the disk surface and destroy more data.
clicking.riskNote: Mechanical faults can get worse every time the drive is powered on, and real repairs need a cleanroom.
stopFirst: Power it off and leave it off. Do not keep trying, because each power-up can scratch the disk inside.
Do not put the drive in the freezer, tap it or shake it. The freezer trick is a myth and can cause water damage from condensation.
Never open the drive. Dust in a normal room ruins the disk.
Do not run recovery scans, CHKDSK or any repair tool on it. Heavy reading stresses a failing drive, and making a copy (see below) is the only DIY step worth trying.

steps.title: Unplug it now
steps.detail: Switching it off stops the damage growing. What you heard is also useful to a professional.
how: Shut down the computer, then unplug the drive's power and data cables, or unplug the USB cable.
Write down what you heard: clicking, grinding, beeping, or no spin at all, and when it started.

steps.title: Decide how valuable the data is
steps.detail: Home attempts can lower the odds for a lab. Knowing the value of your files tells you whether the risk is worth taking.
how: Irreplaceable files such as family photos or work with no backup: skip to the last step and contact a professional.
Replaceable files, or you accept the risk: read on, and plan for at most one careful try.

steps.title: Check the noise really came from the drive
steps.detail: Fans and optical drives can click too. Confirming the source avoids needless worry, and avoids testing cables on a drive that clicks, because clicking is rarely a cable problem.
how: Shut down. Unplug only this drive's power cable.
Start the computer. If the noise is gone, it was the drive.

steps.title: Try one careful attempt, if you accept the risk
steps.detail: A second computer booted from a live USB (a USB stick that runs Linux without installing anything) avoids loading Windows or macOS, which would read the drive heavily as soon as it is connected.
how: Make a live USB using our guide, then boot a second computer from it.
Connect the clicking drive once, with a good cable. Do not retry if it fails.
If it spins and shows up in `lsblk` (a command that lists drives), go straight to making an image. If not, power off.

steps.title: Image it, do not copy it
steps.detail: An image (an exact copy of the whole drive saved as a file) is made by tools that read the easy areas first and skip bad spots, saving the most data before the drive gets worse. Ordinary copy and paste would stall on bad spots and stress the drive.
how: Plug in a healthy destination drive at least as big as the clicking one.
Run ddrescue or HDDSuperClone as shown in the imaging guide. Always type the failing drive first and the empty destination second. If you swap them, the copy erases your data.
Keep the map file ddrescue creates, so it can resume if you must stop.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: Working on the image means the failing drive never has to run again, so you can retry as many times as you need.
how: Power off and unplug the failing drive once imaging is done.
Run TestDisk (for folders and names) on the image file, then PhotoRec if names are lost.
Save recovered files to a third location.

steps.title: Stop at the first sign of trouble, and call a pro
steps.detail: If it clicks, stalls or disappears again, more tries lower what a lab can save. A cleanroom lab can swap the damaged heads, which is not possible at home.
how: Power off at the first stall, click or disappearance.
Do not retry. Pack the drive in a padded box.
Ask a few labs about their price and their policy if they cannot recover anything.

clicking.callPro: If the data matters and the drive clicks, grinds, beeps or will not spin, stop and ask a professional with a cleanroom.

faq.q: Does the freezer trick work?
faq.a: No. It can cause condensation, which is water damage, and make things worse. Data recovery experts advise against it.

faq.q: Can I open the drive and fix it myself?
faq.a: No. Opening a hard drive outside a cleanroom lets in dust that scratches the disk. Replacing the heads needs special tools and matching parts.

faq.q: Is it worth trying once myself?
faq.a: Only if the data is not critical. Keep it to one careful attempt, and make an image straight away if it works.

no-power.title: Hard Drive Not Spinning or Won't Power On
no-power.metaDescription: Hard drive silent, not spinning, or smells burnt? Check power and cables safely, learn why not to retry again and again, and when to see a professional.
no-power.summary: If the drive makes no sound and does not spin, the cause may be a bad cable, a weak power supply, or a failed circuit board or motor. A burnt smell points to an electrical fault, which can be dangerous to keep trying.
no-power.riskNote: Cable and power checks are fine, but repeated attempts on a drive with a burnt board or stuck motor can cause more harm.
stopFirst: Unplug it right away if you smell burning or see scorch marks. Do not power it up again.
Do not switch it on and off again and again hoping it starts. Limit yourself to one or two careful tries.
Do not use the freezer trick, and never open the drive. It needs a cleanroom.
Do not swap circuit boards yourself. Each board has a ROM chip with data unique to that drive, which must be moved over, and that is a job for a lab.

steps.title: Look and smell
steps.detail: Burn marks tell you to stop now, before trying anything else.
how: Shut down and unplug the drive. Turn it over so you can see the green circuit board on the underside.
Look for dark scorch spots, a cracked or blackened chip, and sniff for a burnt smell.
If you see or smell any, leave it unplugged and skip to the last step.

steps.title: Try one other power source
steps.detail: A weak or faulty power supply is a common cause, and trying another is quick and safe.
how: Plug the drive's power into a different connector from the same power supply, or try it in another computer or a USB dock.
Check that other drives on the same cable work. If none do, the power supply is the problem.

steps.title: Use a good data cable for that same try
steps.detail: Swapping the data cable and port in the same attempt tests everything at once, so you power the drive on as few times as possible.
how: Use a spare SATA data cable and a different port on the motherboard, or a USB dock.
Press each connector in firmly before switching on.

steps.title: Listen for spin-up
steps.detail: Spinning up produces a faint hum or vibration. Silence tells you where the fault is.
how: Switch on and rest a fingertip lightly on the drive for about 10 seconds.
Hum or vibration: it spins, so check whether it appears in the BIOS or Disk Management.
Nothing at all: the fault is power, circuit board or motor. Switch off, do not retry.

steps.title: If it spins and shows up, image it
steps.detail: An image (an exact copy of the whole drive saved as a file) lets you recover files without running the shaky drive again and again.
how: Plug in a healthy drive at least as big as this one.
Follow our imaging guide with ddrescue (on Linux), or HDDSuperClone. Always type the failing drive first and the empty destination second. If you swap them, the copy erases your data.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: The image can be searched repeatedly without risk to the original.
how: Run TestDisk to see folders and names, then PhotoRec if needed.
Always point the tools at the image file, never at the original drive.

steps.title: Stop if it stays dead
steps.detail: A drive that never spins needs hardware repair by a professional. More attempts will not help, and they can damage it.
how: Unplug it and pack it in a padded box.
Describe what you saw, heard and smelled when you talk to a lab.
Ask about their price and their policy if they cannot recover anything.

no-power.callPro: If it does not spin after another cable and power source, or there is a burnt smell or scorch marks, stop and call a professional.

faq.q: My drive is dead but not clicking. Is that better or worse?
faq.a: Neither is good. Silence points to power, circuit board or motor trouble. Check the cable and power first, then consider a professional.

faq.q: Can I replace the circuit board myself?
faq.a: Not as a DIY fix. The board's ROM chip holds data unique to that drive and must be moved onto the new board, which experts do with special tools.

faq.q: Is a burnt smell always the end?
faq.a: Not always. Sometimes only a small protection part on the board has blown and the data is fine, but it needs a careful repair by an expert.

liquid-fire.title: Water, Liquid or Fire Damaged Hard Drive
liquid-fire.metaDescription: Hard drive got wet, flooded or burned? Do not power it on, do not use rice or heat. Learn what to do next to give a professional the best chance.
liquid-fire.summary: Liquid can short the circuit board and corrode parts inside, and fire or heat can warp the drive. Switching it on can cause a short or scratch the disk, so the safest move is to keep it off and get professional help.
liquid-fire.riskNote: Power, heat or opening the drive can turn damage that could be fixed into permanent loss.
stopFirst: Do not power it on. Not even once to see if it works.
Do not dry it with a hair dryer, oven or heater, and do not bury it in rice. Heat can warp parts, and rice adds dust and starch without drying the inside.
Do not open the drive or try to clean the disk.
Do not shake it or rinse it to remove dirt or salt water.

steps.title: Keep it unpowered
steps.detail: Power into a wet drive can short the board or scratch the disk. If the drive is inside a laptop or PC, the battery or power supply can be a hazard too.
how: Unplug the power and data cables. For a laptop, unplug the charger and do not press the power button.
Stay away from a swollen, hot or smoking battery. It can catch fire, so move it outdoors on a non-flammable surface if it is safe to do so.
Do not plug it in anywhere to see if it works.

steps.title: Note what happened
steps.detail: What touched the drive decides how fast it corrodes and what the lab needs to do first.
how: Write down whether it was clean water, salt water, a sugary drink, flood mud, smoke or flames, and how long ago.
Take a photo of the drive as it is now, if it is safe to do so.

steps.title: Keep it damp if it came from a flood
steps.detail: Salt and mud eat metal quickly once they dry. Keeping the drive damp stops that until an expert can clean it. Do not dry it out in the open.
how: If it is muddy or salty, place it in a sealed plastic bag as it is. Do not rinse it and do not wipe it.
If it was clean water or a small spill, still do not try to dry it. Just bag it and keep it still.

steps.title: Pack it gently
steps.detail: Knocks can scratch a disk that has been stopped, and heat can warp it.
how: Wrap the drive, still bagged, in a soft cloth.
Put it in a box with padding on all sides and keep it away from heat and sun.

steps.title: Contact a professional soon
steps.detail: Corrosion keeps spreading, so waiting makes recovery harder. Only a lab with a cleanroom can safely open, clean and read the drive.
how: Search for data recovery labs with a cleanroom and ask for a quote before you ship anything.
Ask about their price, their policy if they cannot recover anything, and whether they offer free evaluation.
Send it with tracking and insurance.

liquid-fire.callPro: Water, liquid, smoke or fire damage should go to a professional with a cleanroom before anyone powers the drive on.

faq.q: Will putting it in rice help?
faq.a: No. Rice does not pull water out of a drive, and it can add dust and starch. Keep it off and get professional help.

faq.q: Can I dry it with a hair dryer?
faq.a: No. Heat can warp parts and push moisture further inside. Leave drying and cleaning to an expert.

faq.q: What if it dried and looks fine?
faq.a: Looking fine does not prove it is safe, because leftover residue can short the board. Powering it on is a gamble, so a professional is safer for important data.

corrupted.title: Fix a Corrupted or Unreadable Hard Drive
corrupted.metaDescription: Hard drive corrupted, shows RAW, asks to format, or has read errors? Image it with ddrescue first, then recover files with TestDisk or PhotoRec safely.
corrupted.summary: Corrupted means the drive's records of where each file is are damaged, often after a power cut, a bad shutdown or failing parts. The files are often still there. Do not run repair tools on the original first, because they can change your data.
corrupted.riskNote: The drive may be weakening, and repair tools such as CHKDSK on the original can change data before you have a copy.
stopFirst: Do not run CHKDSK, fsck or Disk Utility's First Aid on the original before copying your data. Repairs can rewrite data.
Do not click Format when Windows says the drive needs to be formatted.
Do not install recovery software onto the affected drive, and do not save recovered files back to it.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: Every extra read or write on a damaged drive risks more damage.
how: Windows: close the drive's folders, then right-click the drive in File Explorer and choose Eject. Mac: drag it to the Trash or click the Eject button in Finder.
Then shut down. If the drive is making clicking or grinding noises, read our clicking guide instead.

steps.title: Check its health
steps.detail: The SMART report is the drive's own health record. It shows whether the disk is wearing out, which decides how gently you must treat it.
how: Windows: install and open CrystalDiskInfo, then look at Health Status. Mac or Linux: in a terminal run `smartctl -a /dev/sdX`.
Reallocated, Pending or Uncorrectable sector counts above zero mean the disk surface is wearing out. Caution or Bad means the drive is failing.

steps.title: Get a second drive that is as large
steps.detail: An image (an exact copy of the whole drive saved as a file) needs as much room as the original drive.
how: Check the damaged drive's size in File Explorer or Disk Utility.
Use a different drive with at least that much free space.

steps.title: Image the drive with ddrescue
steps.detail: ddrescue copies the drive while skipping spots it cannot read and returning to them later. That saves the most data and stresses the drive the least.
how: Boot a live USB if needed (our guide shows how), then open a terminal and run `lsblk` to identify both drives.

Run `sudo ddrescue -n /dev/sdX /mnt/backup/disk.img /mnt/backup/disk.map`, where sdX is the damaged drive. Always type the failing drive first and the empty destination second. If you swap them, the copy erases your data.
Keep the map file so you can stop and resume. HDDSuperClone is an alternative on Linux.

steps.title: Work on the image, not the original
steps.detail: The image is expendable. If a tool changes it, you can make a fresh copy and try again.
how: If you have space, copy the image file so you have a spare.
Run `sudo testdisk disk.img` and follow its menus to rebuild the partition or list the files.
Copy what you find to a different drive.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec as a fallback
steps.detail: If the folder records are too damaged, PhotoRec finds files by their content and saves them with generic names.
how: Run `sudo photorec disk.img` and choose the image file.
Pick the file types you want, then a destination folder on a different drive, and press `c`.

steps.title: Store the recovered files safely
steps.detail: Recovered files are only safe once they are in more than one place.
how: Open a few files of each type to check they work.
Keep a second copy on another drive or in cloud storage.

corrupted.callPro: If imaging keeps stalling, the drive makes noises, or the data is critical, stop and ask a professional rather than hammering the drive.

faq.q: Should I run CHKDSK to fix it?
faq.a: Not first. It can rewrite damaged data. Make an image of the drive, then repair or recover from that copy.

faq.q: What is a disk image?
faq.a: It is an exact copy of everything on the drive, saved as a file or onto another drive. It lets you try recovery over and over without risking the original.

faq.q: Why does it say the drive is RAW?
faq.a: The computer cannot read the drive's file system, which is its way of organising files, usually because of damage. The data is often still there and TestDisk may restore it.

encrypted.title: Recover Data From an Encrypted Hard Drive
encrypted.metaDescription: Locked out of a BitLocker, FileVault or other encrypted hard drive? Find your recovery key first. Without the key or password, recovery is not realistic.
encrypted.summary: Encryption scrambles your data so that only the right password or recovery key can unlock it. If the drive is healthy and you have the key, getting files back is usually simple. Without it, recovery is not realistic, and anyone promising otherwise should not be trusted.
encrypted.riskNote: Unlocking with a known key is low risk, but guessing or tampering with a failing encrypted drive can lock you out for good.
stopFirst: Do not format, reset or reinstall the operating system. That destroys the encryption headers and your chance of unlocking.
Do not keep guessing passwords on a drive that locks you out after failed tries.
Do not trust tools or sites that claim to crack or brute-force strong encryption.

steps.title: Work out which encryption it is
steps.detail: Each kind unlocks differently, so you need to know which you have first.
how: Windows: open File Explorer. A padlock on the drive icon means BitLocker. Mac: a locked drive asks for a password when you open it in Finder, which means FileVault or Mac encryption.
If you are asked for a VeraCrypt password, it is VeraCrypt. On Linux, a prompt for a passphrase at boot usually means LUKS.

steps.title: Find your recovery key
steps.detail: The recovery key is a long backup code made when encryption was turned on. It unlocks the drive if the password fails.
how: BitLocker: sign in at account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey with the Microsoft account you used on the computer. Also check a work or school account.
FileVault: on a Mac, use Apple Account reset on the login screen, or the recovery key you saved.
Also look for a printed page or a text file on a USB stick.

steps.title: Check old notes and password managers
steps.detail: Many people save the key and forget where.
how: Search your email for BitLocker or recovery key.
Check your password manager, printed papers, cloud storage and old USB sticks.
A BitLocker key is a 48-digit number in groups of six digits.

steps.title: Unlock a healthy drive and copy the files
steps.detail: With the key, the drive behaves normally once unlocked, so you can simply copy your files out.
how: Windows: open the drive in File Explorer, click More options, Enter recovery key, and type it in. Mac: enter the password when asked.
Copy your files to a different drive, then open a few to check them.

steps.title: If the drive is also failing, image it first
steps.detail: An image (an exact copy of the whole drive saved as a file) of an encrypted drive stays encrypted, and you unlock the copy later. Only do this if you hold the key.
how: Follow our imaging guide with ddrescue. Always type the failing drive first and the empty destination second. If you swap them, the copy erases your data.
Then unlock the image or a copy with the same key, and copy files out.

steps.title: Accept the limit if no key exists
steps.detail: Modern encryption is designed so that nobody can open it without the key. Recovery tools such as PhotoRec will only return scrambled data.
how: If you have no password and no key, the data cannot realistically be recovered.
If the drive is damaged and you do hold the key, a professional can image it for you.

encrypted.callPro: If you hold the key but the drive is also failing, a professional can make the copy for you. Without the key, no one can realistically recover the data.

faq.q: Where is my BitLocker recovery key?
faq.a: Often in your Microsoft account online, or in a work or school account, a printed page, or a saved file or USB stick.

faq.q: Can someone crack the encryption for me?
faq.a: Not realistically. Modern encryption with a strong password is built to resist this, so be careful of anyone who says otherwise.

faq.q: What if I forgot my FileVault password?
faq.a: Try your Apple Account reset, or the recovery key you saved when you turned it on. Without those, the data cannot be unlocked.

deleted.title: Recover Deleted Photos from an SD or microSD Card
deleted.metaDescription: Deleted photos or videos from an SD or microSD card can often be recovered with PhotoRec. Stop shooting, then follow this safe step-by-step guide.
deleted.summary: When you delete files from an SD card, the card usually just forgets where they were. The photos and videos stay until new ones overwrite them. SD cards do not use TRIM (a feature that wipes deleted space) in most cameras and readers, so recovery odds are often good. The most important step is to stop using the card.
deleted.riskNote: Scanning a copy is safe, but taking even a few more photos can overwrite what you want back.
stopFirst: Stop taking photos or videos with the card right now. New ones can overwrite the old.
Do not install recovery software onto the card.
Do not format the card, even if the camera or phone asks you to.

steps.title: Remove the card
steps.detail: Even leaving the card in a powered-on device can save small files onto it.
how: Turn the camera or phone off.
Open the card door or tray and take the card out. A microSD card may need a pin or fingernail.
Do not put it back in any device until recovery is finished.

steps.title: Check backups
steps.detail: A backup can save you the whole recovery.
how: Phone: open Google Photos, iCloud Photos or OneDrive and check the Recently Deleted or Trash area.
Camera with two card slots: check the second card.
Check your computer and any old backup drives for copies you imported earlier.

steps.title: Use a card reader and lock the card
steps.detail: A card reader lets the computer read the card without the camera or phone writing to it. Locking the card tells the computer to treat it as read-only, which protects your photos.
how: Take the card out of the camera or phone. A microSD card sits in a small slot or tray, so use a pin or fingernail if needed.
Full-size SD card or a microSD adapter: slide the small lock switch on the side down to the Lock position, before you plug it in. A plain microSD card has no switch.
Put the card in a USB card reader and plug it into the computer. Some readers ignore the lock, so still do not save anything to the card.
If a window offers to format the card, click Cancel. Never click Format.

steps.title: Make an image of the SD card
steps.detail: An image is an exact copy of the whole SD card saved as one file. You then run every recovery tool on the copy, so the original is never touched again. ddrescue is the free tool that makes the copy and keeps going past unreadable spots. Do this before trying any recovery tool. Type the SD card first and the destination second; swapping them erases the SD card.
how: You need a second drive with free space at least as big as the SD card. Plug it in and note its name.

Windows: ddrescue runs from Linux, so follow the Live USB guide to start your PC from a Linux USB stick (a stick that starts a temporary Linux without touching your drive). Mac: press Cmd+Space, type Terminal, press Enter, then type `brew install ddrescue` (needs Homebrew from brew.sh).
Find the SD card's name. Linux: type `lsblk` and match it by size (it looks like /dev/sdb). Mac: type `diskutil list` (it looks like /dev/disk4). Pick by size, never guess.
Mac only: type `diskutil unmountDisk /dev/disk4` (use your number) so the Mac lets go of it. Do not click Initialize or Erase if a window pops up.

Type `sudo ddrescue -d /dev/sdX /mnt/backup/sdcard.img /mnt/backup/map.log` replacing sdX and the folder with yours. The first path is the SD card (the source), the second is where the copy goes. Swapping them erases the SD card.
Wait until it says it is finished. Keep the map.log file: it lets you stop and resume. Work only on an image file from now on.

steps.title: Try TestDisk
steps.detail: TestDisk can list deleted files with their original names. It is quick and worth a try.
how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). Windows: unzip the download from cgsecurity.org and double-click `testdisk_win.exe`. Mac or Linux: in Terminal type `sudo testdisk`.

If you made an image, open it by typing `testdisk image.img` (Windows: run this in Command Prompt from the TestDisk folder). Otherwise choose the drive from the list with the arrow keys and press Enter.
Choose `Create` (log file), then pick the partition table type it suggests, usually `Intel/PC` or `EFI GPT`, and press Enter.
Choose your partition, then `Advanced` and `Undelete`. Deleted files show in red. Press `c` to copy one and pick a folder on a different drive.
Use the arrow keys and Enter to move around and `q` to go back. TestDisk only changes anything if you choose Write, so do not choose it yet.

steps.title: Run PhotoRec
steps.detail: PhotoRec finds photos and videos, including many camera RAW formats (the untouched files some cameras save), even if the file list is gone.
how: Open PhotoRec (a free tool that searches for file contents instead of file names). Windows: unzip the TestDisk download and double-click `qphotorec_win.exe` for the click-and-type window. Mac or Linux: in Terminal type `sudo photorec`.
Choose your image file (or the drive if you have no image) at the top of the window or in the list, then pick `Whole disk` or the biggest partition.
Click `File Formats` and untick types you do not need (for example keep only JPG, PNG, MP4, DOCX) to save time. Skipping this is also fine.
Click `Browse` and choose a folder on a folder on your computer or a different drive, never the card itself, never on the drive you are scanning.
Click `Search` (terminal: press `C`). It can take hours. Leave the computer on.

steps.title: Save somewhere else
steps.detail: If you save back onto the card, you could overwrite photos you have not recovered yet.
how: When asked for a destination, pick a folder on your computer's main drive or another external drive.
Make sure it has more free space than the card's size.
Never choose the card or its image file as the destination.
Then open a few photos to check them. Windows: double-click them. Mac: press Space on a file for a preview.

deleted.callPro: If the card disconnects during copying, or irreplaceable photos do not turn up, stop and ask a professional.

faq.q: Can I recover photos I deleted from a camera card?
faq.a: Often yes, if you stopped using the card. Photos are usually still on it until new ones overwrite them.

faq.q: Does taking more photos hurt my chances?
faq.a: Yes. New pictures can be written over the deleted ones, so stop using the card immediately.

formatted.summary: Formatting in most cameras clears the file list (the index of what is stored where) but leaves most photos on the card. Formatting in a phone, a full format in Windows, or a camera's 'low-level' or 'secure' format often erases the data and lowers the odds.
formatted.riskNote: Recovery scans are safe on a copy, but taking new photos or formatting again overwrites the old data.
stopFirst: Do not take any more photos or videos with the card.
Do not format it again or choose a 'secure' or 'full' format.
Do not install recovery software onto the card.

steps.title: Remove the card

how: Switch the camera or phone off.
Take the card out. A microSD card may need a pin or fingernail.
Do not put it back in the device.

steps.title: Look for the old layout
steps.detail: A partition is a section of the card that holds your files. TestDisk can often find the layout from before the format.
how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). Windows: unzip the download from cgsecurity.org and double-click `testdisk_win.exe`. Mac or Linux: in Terminal type `sudo testdisk`.

steps.title: Scan with PhotoRec
steps.detail: If TestDisk cannot find the old layout, PhotoRec pulls out photos, videos and documents by their contents. File names are lost.
