steps.title: Save to another drive and check
steps.detail: Saving on a different disk keeps the card safe, and opening samples proves the photos are not damaged.
how: Recover to a folder on your computer or another external drive.
Open the recovered folder. PhotoRec makes `recup_dir.1`, `recup_dir.2` and so on.
Windows: double-click photos to open them. Mac: select one and press Space.
Photos that open fine are good. Gray or broken ones are damaged.

formatted.callPro: If the card was fully formatted, reused heavily, or will not copy, a professional may help, but chances are lower.

faq.q: Do formatted SD cards keep my photos?
faq.a: Usually a quick format does. Most photos remain until new ones are written, so recovery is often possible.

faq.q: Should I format the card again to fix it?
faq.a: Not until your files are safely recovered. Another format can overwrite more data.

not-detected.title: SD or microSD Card Not Detected or Not Reading
not-detected.metaDescription: SD or microSD card not showing up? Try a different reader, check the lock switch, and learn when a dead card needs professional chip-level help.
not-detected.summary: A card may not show up because of a dirty or bad reader, a missing drive letter, damaged file information, or a failed controller (the tiny chip that runs the card). not-detected.riskNote: Simple checks are safe, but accepting a format prompt or forcing a damaged card can destroy what is left.
stopFirst: Do not click Format when the computer or camera asks.
Do not bend, force or clean the card contacts with anything rough.
Do not keep inserting and removing it many times.

steps.title: Try another reader
steps.detail: A faulty reader or adapter is a very common cause. It is a free, safe test.
how: Plug the card into a different USB card reader, in a different USB port.
microSD: also try a different SD adapter.
Try another computer. If a window offers to format, click Cancel.
Check the lock switch on a full-size SD card is not stuck halfway.

steps.title: Look in Disk Management or Disk Utility
steps.detail: These tools list every drive, even one with no drive letter or an unreadable format (shown as RAW).
how: Windows: right-click the Start button and choose Disk Management. Mac: press Cmd+Space, type Disk Utility and press Enter, then click View > Show All Devices.
Look for a drive about the size of your card.
Do not click Initialize, Format or Delete. Just note what appears.
A card with no letter or showing RAW may still hold your files.

steps.title: Clean gently
steps.detail: Dust or film on the gold contacts can stop the reader seeing the card.

Wipe the gold contacts with a dry, soft, lint-free cloth.
Do not use liquid, erasers or a knife.
Try the reader again once.

steps.title: Recover from the image

how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). Windows: unzip the download from cgsecurity.org and double-click `testdisk_win.exe`. Mac or Linux: in Terminal type `sudo testdisk`.

steps.title: Ask a professional if it never appears
steps.detail: If no reader detects the card, or it shows a tiny size such as 0 MB, the controller or memory has likely failed. Most microSD cards are sealed monolith chips (chip and controller in one piece), which need a lab with flash recovery tools.
how: Decide how valuable the files are. If they cannot be replaced, stop experimenting.
Search for data recovery labs near you. Look for a free evaluation and a 'no data, no fee' promise.
Describe your exact problem and ask for a price range before you send anything.
Pack the device in an anti-static bag or bubble wrap and ship it only after you agree on terms.

not-detected.callPro: If no reader detects the card, or it shows 0 MB, a lab with flash recovery tools is your only option.

faq.q: Why does my microSD card show nothing in the reader?
faq.a: The reader, adapter or card contacts may be bad, or the card's controller may have failed. Try a different reader first.

faq.q: Can a dead SD card be recovered?
faq.a: Sometimes, by labs that read the memory directly, often by soldering to tiny test points on monolith cards. It is costly and not guaranteed.

no-power.title: SD or microSD Card Dead and Not Responding
no-power.metaDescription: SD or microSD card completely dead? Rule out the reader and adapter, then learn why a failed controller needs a lab with special flash recovery tools.
no-power.summary: A card has no light or sound, so a dead card simply does not respond anywhere. Check the reader, adapter and contacts first. If it is still dead, the controller (the tiny chip that runs the card) is likely broken, and the data can only be read with special equipment.
no-power.riskNote: A cracked or shorted card can be damaged further by repeated tries, and DIY opening or soldering destroys it.
stopFirst: Do not keep trying if the card feels hot or looks cracked.
Do not open the card or try to solder it.
Do not format it if it briefly appears and asks.

steps.title: Swap the reader and adapter
steps.detail: Most 'dead' cards are really a bad reader or adapter.
how: Test your reader with a different card you know works. If that fails too, the reader is the problem.
microSD: try another SD adapter.
Try a different USB port.
Do this once or twice, not repeatedly.

steps.title: Check the card visually
steps.detail: Physical damage means more tries could do harm.
how: Hold the card in good light.
Look for cracks, bent plastic, burn marks and missing or scratched gold contacts.
If you see damage, stop and go to the professional step.

steps.title: Try a second computer
steps.detail: A different computer or operating system sometimes reads what the first cannot.
how: Plug the card into a different computer, ideally with a different operating system.

If a window offers to format the card, click Cancel.

deleted.title: Recover Deleted Files from an SSD

deleted.riskNote: Scanning is safe if you save results to a different drive, but while the SSD stays powered on, your computer can save new files or run TRIM again and erase what is left.

Do not install any recovery program onto the SSD you want files back from. It would write over the very files you want.
Do not run disk cleanup, 'optimize' or 'trim' tools. They tell the SSD to wipe deleted space.

steps.detail: The sooner the SSD loses power, the less time it has to wipe deleted data in the background. A full shutdown matters more than logging out or closing the lid.

formatted.riskNote: Reinstalling Windows or saving new files on the SSD speeds up permanent loss, so careless steps can end any chance of recovery.

Do not install recovery software on the formatted SSD.

steps.title: Power down
steps.detail: SSDs keep tidying and wiping in the background while powered. Turning the computer off stops that.

not-detected.title: SSD Not Detected or Not Showing Up

steps.detail: Many 'dead' SSDs are actually bad cables, adapters or USB enclosures (small cases that turn an SSD into a USB drive).

liquid-fire.riskNote: Powering on or heat-drying a damaged SSD can short the board and destroy data that was otherwise safe.
stopFirst: Do not plug the SSD in or turn on the device it is in.
Do not rinse it or dry it with a hair dryer, oven, rice or any heat.
Do not shake it, clean the contacts or open it.

steps.title: Disconnect power
steps.detail: Cutting power stops a short circuit from doing more harm. Safety comes first.
how: Turn the device off. If it is already off, leave it off.
Unplug the charger.
Remove the battery and the SSD only if they come out easily without tools. Do not force anything.
If the battery is swollen, hot or smoking, do not touch it. Move away and call the fire service.

steps.detail: Handling the SSD roughly or wiping it can spread residue and bend parts. Rinsing is dangerous because it can carry dirt and salts further in.
how: Pick the SSD up by the edges. Do not touch the gold contacts.
Put it in a clean, dry, anti-static bag (the shiny bag electronics come in) or a small box. A zip bag with no moisture is also fine.

steps.detail: A recovery lab chooses its cleaning method based on what the SSD was exposed to.
how: Write down the liquid (fresh water, salt water, coffee, sugary drink, smoke) or heat source.
Note how long it was wet or hot, and whether it was powered on at the time.
Note the drive's make, model and size from its label.
Keep the note with the drive.

steps.detail: A backup means you may not need a lab at all.

Ask about a free evaluation and 'no data, no fee' terms before you pay.

Move to a file or folder with the arrow keys and press `c` to copy it.

encrypted.title: Recover Data from an Encrypted SSD
encrypted.metaDescription: Encrypted SSDs need the password or recovery key. Find BitLocker, FileVault or VeraCrypt keys and learn why brute force is not a real option.
encrypted.summary: If your SSD is protected with BitLocker (Windows), FileVault (Mac), VeraCrypt or built-in hardware encryption, the data is scrambled without the key. encrypted.riskNote: Wrong attempts, resets, or erasing the drive's encryption can make the data permanently unreadable.
stopFirst: Do not reset, secure erase or 'crypto erase' the SSD. That destroys the key and the data for good.

steps.title: Identify the encryption type
steps.detail: The kind of encryption decides where the key is stored and how to unlock the drive.
how: Windows: open File Explorer. A padlock on the drive icon means BitLocker.

steps.title: Find the recovery key
steps.detail: A recovery key is a code saved when encryption was turned on. It unlocks the drive when the password is lost.

Search your email for 'recovery key' and 'BitLocker'.
Check notes apps, cloud notes and old documents.
Ask family or IT staff who may have set it up.

Mac only: type `diskutil unmountDisk /dev/disk4` (use your number) so the Mac lets go of it. Do not click Initialize or Erase if a window pops up.

Type `sudo ddrescue -d /dev/sdX /mnt/backup/usbdrive.img /mnt/backup/map.log` replacing sdX and the folder with yours. The first path is the USB drive (the source), the second is where the copy goes. Swapping them erases the USB drive.
Wait until it says it is finished. Keep the map.log file: it lets you stop and resume. Work only on an image file from now on.

steps.title: Recover from the copy
steps.detail: TestDisk and PhotoRec search the copy for your files, so the fragile drive is not used again.
how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). Windows: unzip the download from cgsecurity.org and double-click `testdisk_win.exe`. Mac or Linux: in Terminal type `sudo testdisk`.

If you made an image, open it by typing `testdisk image.img` (Windows: run this in Command Prompt from the TestDisk folder). Otherwise choose the drive from the list with the arrow keys and press Enter.
Choose `Create` (log file), then pick the partition table type it suggests, usually `Intel/PC` or `EFI GPT`, and press Enter.
Choose `Analyse`, then `Quick Search`, and copy found files to another drive. If nothing shows, run PhotoRec on the image.
Use the arrow keys and Enter to move around and `q` to go back. TestDisk only changes anything if you choose Write, so do not choose it yet.

steps.title: Get professional help
steps.detail: Burns, corrosion or a drive that will not appear after drying call for a lab. Labs have tools to clean the board and read the chip safely.
how: Decide how valuable the files are. If they cannot be replaced, stop experimenting.
Search for data recovery labs near you. Look for a free evaluation and a 'no data, no fee' promise.
Describe your exact problem and ask for a price range before you send anything.
Pack the device in an anti-static bag or bubble wrap and ship it only after you agree on terms.

liquid-fire.callPro: If it is burned, cracked, corroded or not detected after drying, stop and call a professional.

faq.q: Can a USB drive survive the washing machine?
faq.a: Often yes, if it is fully dried before use. Waiting several days is safer than plugging it in right away.

faq.q: Is heat drying safe for a flash drive?
faq.a: No. Heat can damage the memory chip and the solder joints.

corrupted.title: Fix a Corrupted USB Flash Drive Without Data Loss
corrupted.metaDescription: USB drive says RAW, asks to format, or files will not open? Image it first, then use TestDisk and PhotoRec. Do not format or run chkdsk yet.
corrupted.summary: A corrupted USB drive has damaged file system information (the index of what is stored where). It often shows as RAW, meaning the computer cannot read how it is organized, usually after being pulled out too early or from worn memory. The files are often still there. Making a copy before any repair keeps your options open.
corrupted.riskNote: Formatting or running chkdsk can overwrite the information you need, and a failing drive may get worse with each use.
stopFirst: Do not click Format when Windows asks you to. That wipes the index you need.
Do not run chkdsk or any 'repair' prompt before making an image.
Do not install recovery software onto the USB drive.

steps.title: Stop and unplug
steps.detail: Prompts that offer to repair or format change the drive. Declining them keeps your files safe.
how: If a window says you need to format the disk, click Cancel.
Windows: eject from the arrow near the clock. Mac: right-click the drive > Eject.
Do not click Check Disk, Scan and Fix, or First Aid yet.

steps.detail: An image is an exact copy of the whole USB drive saved as one file. You then run every recovery tool on the copy, so the original is never touched again. ddrescue is the free tool that makes the copy and keeps going past unreadable spots. This also shows which areas are unreadable. Type the USB drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases the USB drive.

Wait until it says it is finished. Keep the map.log file: it lets you stop and resume. Work only on an image file from now on.

steps.title: Try TestDisk on the image
steps.detail: A partition is a section of the drive. TestDisk can find a lost one or repair a damaged boot sector (the part that says how the drive starts).
how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). Windows: unzip the download from cgsecurity.org and double-click `testdisk_win.exe`. Mac or Linux: in Terminal type `sudo testdisk`.

If you made an image, open it by typing `testdisk image.img` (Windows: run this in Command Prompt from the TestDisk folder). Otherwise choose the drive from the list with the arrow keys and press Enter.
Choose `Create` (log file), then pick the partition table type it suggests, usually `Intel/PC` or `EFI GPT`, and press Enter.
Choose `Analyse`, then `Quick Search`. If your folders appear, press `p` to browse and `c` to copy files to a different drive. Do not choose `Write`.
Use the arrow keys and Enter to move around and `q` to go back. TestDisk only changes anything if you choose Write, so do not choose it yet.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec if folders are lost
steps.detail: PhotoRec recovers files by type from the image. Names and folders are not kept.
how: Open PhotoRec (a free tool that searches for file contents instead of file names). Windows: unzip the TestDisk download and double-click `qphotorec_win.exe` for the click-and-type window. Mac or Linux: in Terminal type `sudo photorec`.
Choose your image file (or the drive if you have no image) at the top of the window or in the list, then pick `Whole disk` or the biggest partition.
Click `File Formats` and untick types you do not need (for example keep only JPG, PNG, MP4, DOCX) to save time. Skipping this is also fine.
Click `Browse` and choose a folder on a folder on your computer or a different drive, never the USB drive itself, never on the drive you are scanning.
Click `Search` (terminal: press `C`). It can take hours. Leave the computer on.

steps.title: Save to a different drive
steps.detail: Saving back onto the USB drive would overwrite your files.
how: Choose a folder on your computer or another external drive.
Make sure there is enough free space.
Open a few files to make sure they work.

steps.title: Fix the USB last
steps.detail: Only after your files are safe is it fine to wipe the drive. Flash memory wears out, so a drive that keeps corrupting should be replaced.
how: Windows: right-click the drive in File Explorer > Format > Start. Mac: Disk Utility > select the drive > Erase.
This erases everything, so check your recovered files first.
If the drive keeps corrupting later, buy a new one and stop using this one.

corrupted.callPro: If copying keeps failing, the drive disconnects or it shows the wrong size, stop and ask a professional.

faq.q: Why does my USB say I need to format the disk?
faq.a: The file system information is damaged. Your files may still be present, so do not format until you have a copy.

faq.q: Is it safe to run chkdsk on a corrupted USB drive?
faq.a: Not before you have a copy. Chkdsk changes the drive and can delete data it cannot fix.

encrypted.title: Recover Data from an Encrypted USB Drive
encrypted.metaDescription: Locked USB drive from BitLocker To Go, VeraCrypt or a hardware PIN? Without the key recovery is not realistic. Learn where keys are often saved.
encrypted.summary: Encrypted USB drives scramble data so it cannot be read without the password or recovery key (a long code saved when encryption was turned on). If you have neither, recovery is not realistic. Many people can find the key in a Microsoft account or a password manager.
encrypted.riskNote: Wrong resets or an erase on a hardware-encrypted stick can destroy the key and make the data permanently unreadable.
stopFirst: Do not reset the drive or keep guessing its PIN. Many keypad drives wipe themselves after a set number of wrong tries.
Do not format it to get access. That erases the data.
Do not use tools that claim to crack or guess encryption.

steps.title: Identify the type
steps.detail: How it was locked decides where the key is.
how: Plug the drive in. Windows: a padlock on the drive icon in File Explorer means BitLocker To Go.
A drive with a keypad on its case uses hardware encryption.
A drive holding a program or file called VeraCrypt uses VeraCrypt.
Check the drive's label or box for a vendor name and look up its manual.

steps.title: Find the key
steps.detail: BitLocker recovery keys are usually saved online or printed.
how: BitLocker: sign in at account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey with your Microsoft account. Also check any work or school account.
Look for a printout, or a text file on another drive or in email.
A BitLocker key is 48 digits in 8 groups.
Match the key ID on the lock screen to the one shown online.

steps.title: Search your passwords
steps.detail: The password is often in a manager, notes or an email.
how: Search your password manager for the drive name, BitLocker or VeraCrypt.
Search email and notes for 'recovery key'.
Check old documents and sticky notes.

steps.title: Unlock normally
steps.detail: Once you have the key, unlocking is the safe way in.
how: Plug the drive into a working computer.
Windows (BitLocker): double-click the drive, click More options > Enter recovery key, type it and click Unlock.
VeraCrypt: open the VeraCrypt app, click Select Device, pick the drive, click Mount and enter the password.
Copy the files to another drive.

steps.title: Run recovery after unlocking
steps.detail: If files are missing, TestDisk and PhotoRec can search the unlocked volume or its image.
how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). Windows: unzip the download from cgsecurity.org and double-click `testdisk_win.exe`. Mac or Linux: in Terminal type `sudo testdisk`.

If you made an image, open it by typing `testdisk image.img` (Windows: run this in Command Prompt from the TestDisk folder). Otherwise choose the drive from the list with the arrow keys and press Enter.

Point TestDisk or PhotoRec at the unlocked drive or image, choose `Analyse` and `Quick Search`, and copy files to another drive.
Use the arrow keys and Enter to move around and `q` to go back. TestDisk only changes anything if you choose Write, so do not choose it yet.

encrypted.callPro: If the drive is encrypted and failing, or its hardware controller has died, ask a professional and expect it may not be possible.

faq.q: Can I recover files from a locked USB without the password?
faq.a: Realistically no. Good encryption cannot be bypassed, and anyone who promises otherwise should be treated with caution.

faq.q: Where is my BitLocker key stored?
faq.a: Often in your Microsoft account online, in a work or school account, on a printout or in a file you saved earlier.
